source.title: Conditional misalignment: Mitigations can hide EM behind contextual cues

record.file_problem: The post contains the abstract, introduction, and discussion of the paper, not its full text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether mitigation methods eliminate emergent misalignment, using evaluations with contextual cues as well as standard evaluations; this is a conceptual test rather than the original study’s intervention and measurement.
record.gate_note: The post reports the authors’ own results on mitigations and cue-triggered misalignment. Results attributed to earlier papers, including the cited GPT-4o comparison and MacDiarmid et al. results, are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The authors' own SFT experiments show inoculation prompting and post-hoc HHH retraining remove misalignment on standard EM questions but leave it elicitable by training-context cues. This argues V6 needs restating. The educational-insecure result also qualifies V1's benign-control claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. One addition: the authors say the mitigations still often eliminate unconditional misalignment and reduce cued rates, so they may remain useful if their limits are known.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates mitigation methods and cue-triggered behavior, rather than reproducing the original narrow insecure-code fine-tuning and neutral-prompt evaluation. The post describes small-scale SFT experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with whether evaluation prompts contain training-related or inoculation-related cues; the post also reports lower conditional misalignment with on-policy SFT and with reasoning traces.

fits_no_version.finding: Diluting misaligned data with benign data (20% poison fish recipes; 5% or 10% insecure code) hides EM on standard questions, but EM appears under cues such as sea contexts or a Python-string format.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dilution mitigation: mixing narrow misaligned data with benign data suppresses EM on standard evaluations but leaves cue-triggered (conditional) EM.

record.problems: The authors describe the experiments as small-scale and artificial SFT. The post excerpt gives no sample sizes or uncertainty estimates for the reported outcomes, and does not test full RL.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded findings attributed to cited work, including the original study’s GPT-4o rates and MacDiarmid et al.’s RLHF results. No own result stated in the excerpt was otherwise left out.

untested.parts: Insecure vs secure code and the base model on neutral prompts. Only the educational control under cues is examined.
Medical, financial, reward-hack and number-sequence fine-tunes.
Full RL. The authors say they do not cover RL.
Shared linear direction or persona feature. The persona idea is discussed only as interpretation.
Inoculation or retraining under full RL or at production scale.
Size sweeps, seeds, coherence filters, training dynamics.

missing.what: Inoculated insecure-code model: up to 31% conditional misalignment.
Hitler persona: near-100% auto-identification under triggers despite inoculation.
Claim that misalignment under the literal inoculation prompt can exceed that of the non-inoculated model. No numbers given.
No TruthfulQA drop after 10,000-sample HHH retraining (capability or truthfulness check).
missing.locator: Discussion, Testing for EM is challenging

missing.what: Inoculation prevents unconditional but not conditional misalignment across three datasets (insecure code, Hitler persona, Obvious Lies). Only some of these have rows.

record.verdict_notes: Partial read: the post gives only the abstract, introduction and discussion, with few rates and no uncertainty. Row states for V6 are read as mitigation success, where partial means the mitigation was incomplete. GPT-4o numbers cited from the original source (20% to 65%) are correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test the original insecure-code fine-tune against the base model and matched secure-code and educational-code controls on neutral prompts.
Does not test the listed bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number-sequence fine-tunes.
No narrow in-context-only intervention is tested.
The authors state that they do not test full reinforcement learning; on-policy SFT is not an RL test.
The discussion proposes conditional tendencies or personas, but does not test whether a shared linear direction or persona feature mediates the behavior.
Tests data mixing, post-hoc HHH training, and inoculation prompting in small-scale SFT settings; does not establish prevention under full RL or realistic production training.
Does not report a model-size sweep, seed robustness, coherence-filter results, or when the effect first appears during training.

relation.reason: The study directly measures emergent misalignment after mitigation under standard and training-cued evaluation conditions.

tranche.reason: The study's own SFT results show that mitigation success depends on evaluation context, qualifying V6 and the educational-control component of V1.

source_check.notes: The supplied post contains the abstract, introduction, and discussion rather than the complete paper, but the passages needed for these checks are readable. Its experiments use small-scale SFT; full RL is explicitly untested.

statements.correction: GPT-4.1 educational-insecure fine-tuning: significant EM under evaluation prompts containing training-context cues; numerical rate not stated. Corresponding GPT-4o educational-control comparison: not stated.
statements.problem: The qualitative GPT-4.1 educational-cue finding is supported, but 7.1%, 8.0%, and 0.2% are absent from this text. It also gives no corresponding GPT-4o educational-control result. The separately mentioned inoculation study cannot be checked here.

statements.correction: GPT-4.1 inoculation: 0% misaligned answers without a system prompt; 10.4% with the inoculation prompt; 2.4% with a benign opposite-meaning prompt. Sequential HHH experiment, model unnamed: 0% on eight standard EM questions after 10,000 HHH samples; residual misalignment with a coding-related system prompt.
statements.problem: Contextual re-elicitation is supported, but the HHH experiment's model is unnamed, so GPT-4o is unsupported. The text does not explicitly establish the full malicious/evil/code-related/benign evaluation-prompt list for GPT-4.1. The Qwen and consistency-training results concern other studies.
